title: Classification metrics: confusion matrix, precision & recall
intro: The confusion matrix as the foundation, accuracy and why it misleads, precision and recall, the F1 score — and binary cross-entropy as the training objective.
keyPoints: Everything starts with the confusion matrix: TP, FP, FN and TN.
Accuracy can mislead on imbalanced classes — 99% accurate may mean 'always the majority'.
Precision: of my positive predictions, how many were right? Recall: of the true positives, how many did I find?
F1 = the harmonic mean of precision and recall; BCE is the loss the model minimises in training.
Moving the threshold shifts the balance between precision and recall.

blocks.html: Every standard metric builds on one table: the confusion matrix, crossing predictions with reality — each prediction lands in exactly one of four cells.
TP = rightful alarm, TN = rightful all-clear, FP = false alarm, FN = missed case. The asymmetry: in medical screening a missed case is worse; in a spam filter a false alarm is.
The matrix itself is a diagnostic: many FPs = too eager (threshold too low); many FNs = too cautious — the threshold shifts the balance.

sections.title: Accuracy — and why it can mislead

blocks.label: accuracy
blocks.caption: The share of predictions that is correct — all taken together.

blocks.html: The danger: imbalanced classes. At 99% non-spam, “always non-spam” also scores 99% accuracy — and is completely useless. Hence precision and recall.
Rule of thumb: with imbalanced classes (e.g. 1% fraud, 5% disease) accuracy says almost nothing. Always look at precision and recall — or at the confusion matrix itself.

sections.title: Precision & recall: the two sides of the error

blocks.html: Precision: of everything you called positive, how much truly was? Recall: of everything truly positive, how much did you find?

blocks.label: precision
blocks.caption: Of everything I called positive: how much was truly positive? Important when a false alarm is expensive.

blocks.label: recall
blocks.caption: Of everything that is truly positive: how much did I find? Important when you must not miss anything.

rows: a false alarm = an important email in the trash
damage accumulates with every missed fraud
irrelevant suggestions cost trust and attention

blocks.html: They are in tension: stricter threshold = fewer FPs (precision up) but more FNs (recall down). The right balance depends on the costs of both error types.
Precision and recall in one number? Not the plain mean (extremes 1.0 and 0.0 still average 0.5), but the harmonic mean:

blocks.label: F1-score
blocks.caption: The harmonic mean of precision and recall — a balance between the two.

blocks.html: The harmonic mean punishes extremes: one low value drags F1 down. High only if both are high.
The four functions take true and predicted classes (0/1, threshold already applied) and count TP/FP/TN/FN with boolean masks. scikit-learn ships them — seeing the construction makes them concrete.

blocks.caption: implementing accuracy, precision, recall & F1

blocks.html: This is how the counting works: tp = np.sum((y_true == 1) & (y_pred == 1)) — a boolean mask that is only true where both are 1, and np.sum counts the Trues. Watch out for division by zero: if there is no positive prediction at all, precision is undefined.

sections.title: Binary cross-entropy: the loss behind the classifier

blocks.html: The metrics above judge the decision after the threshold; during training the objective is binary cross-entropy (BCE) — \( y \) the classes (1/0), \( \hat{y} \) the predicted probabilities.

blocks.label: binary cross-entropy
blocks.caption: Punishes predicted probabilities that lie far from the true class, logarithmically hard.

blocks.html: Why this shape? For \( y = 1 \), \( -\log(\hat{y}) \) punishes probabilities toward 0; for \( y = 0 \), \( -\log(1-\hat{y}) \) punishes probabilities toward 1. One function, two directions, smooth and minimizable.

blocks.caption: implementing BCE
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def bce(y_true, y_pred):
    # prevent log(0) — these two lines are fixed
    epsilon = 1e-15
    y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, epsilon, 1 - epsilon)

    # the formula from the theory, copied directly
    return -np.mean(y_true * np.log(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) * np.log(1 - y_pred))

# example: good probabilities = low loss
y_true = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0])
y_pred = np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.8, 0.3])

print('bce:', bce(y_true, y_pred))  # 0.19763488164214868

# same labels, confident mistakes = high loss
y_bad = np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.2, 0.8])
print('bce (wrong):', bce(y_true, y_bad))

blocks.html: Probabilities near the correct labels = low BCE; confident mistakes = high. This is the learning signal that shifts the coefficients.

sections.title: From probability to decision: the threshold

blocks.html: From probability to decision in four steps: (1) linear score \( l \), (2) sigmoid → probability, (3) threshold (usually 0.5), (4) minimize BCE during training. The threshold is adjustable and shifts the precision/recall balance.
Below: logistic regression with two features. Slide b0 and b1 and watch the boundary trade one error type for the other — the live metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) recompute on every move.

blocks.title: Dataset A — linearly separable
blocks.subtitle: The two classes are well separated: a straight line exists that separates them perfectly. Find it — the chips turn green once accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are all 1.

blocks.title: Dataset B — overlapping classes
blocks.subtitle: The clouds overlap: no straight line separates them perfectly. Every boundary trades false positives for false negatives. Best achievable here: accuracy 0.75 (precision 0.88 / recall 0.58) — drag and watch the metrics move along.

blocks.html: Dataset B shows the essence: overlapping clouds → no boundary is perfect, every shift trades FPs for FNs. For non-linearly separated data: transform features (e.g. \( x_1^2, x_2^2 \)) or use a kernel.
